title: Tokyo train station will play Godzilla theme song as new departure melody
description: Japanese subway company adds a new soundscape to Godzilla’s Tokyo home. November 3 is a special date for fans of Godzilla as it’s known as “Godzilla Day”. First celebrated to mark the anniversary of the premiere date of the original 1954 film, Godzilla, it was eventually adopted by Toho, the film’s production company, and after it […]
content:
Japanese subway company adds a new soundscape to Godzilla’s Tokyo home.

November 3 is a special date for fans of Godzilla as it’s known as “Godzilla Day”. First celebrated to mark the anniversary of the premiere date of the original 1954 film, Godzilla, it was eventually adopted by Toho, the film’s production company, and after it was registered with the Japan Anniversary Association in 2017, Godzilla Day was officially established, representing Godzilla’s birthday.

While it’s heartening to know the kaiju has a day of its own, it also brings up a unique set of challenges, like…. what the heck do you give the King of the Monsters for his birthday? Well, subway operator Tokyo Metro has come up with a beautiful way to mark the occasion, by changing the departure melody for its trains at Hibiya Station to “Godzilla’s Theme”.

▼ Hibiya Station

Originally composed by Akira Ifukube for the 1954 film, “Godzilla’s Theme” is one of the most instantly recognisable pieces of Godzilla-associated music, with brass, strings and percussion instruments playing a relentless march that’s equal parts call-to-arms inspiring and run-for-your-life fear-inducing.

Two versions of the melody are set to be played, with different arrangements used depending on which direction you’re travelling. One arrangement will be played on platforms 1 and 3, which serves Hibiya Line trains bound for Naka-meguro and Chiyoda Line trains bound for Yoyogi-Uehara, while the other arrangement will play on platforms 2 and 4, for trains heading towards Kita-senju and Ayase.

▼ Hibiya Station is conveniently located in the heart of Tokyo.

Like all departure melodies, these ones will be played just before the train doors close and the train departs, so as long as you’re on the platform at the time you’ll be able to hear it. Tokyo Metro is asking fans to avoid lingering on the platforms though, and it’s also requesting that they avoid crowding around the speakers to record the melodies or in any other spots that might interfere with station operations.

There’s a high likelihood that fans of Godzilla will be arriving and departing by train, though, as Hibiya itself is closely tied to the kaiju, being home to Toho’s headquarters. Toho has been producing the Godzilla series for more than 70 years, and nods to the famous local company are present in two statues, one of which stands at Hibiya Godzilla Square and the other at Toho Cinemas Hibiya.

▼ Hibiya Godzilla Square

▼ The Hibiya statues are a lot smaller than this giant Godzilla atop Shinjuku Toho Building, which houses Toho Cinemas Shinjuku.

For a lot of fans, Hibiya has already established itself as Godzilla’s stomping ground, so the new departure melodies are an exciting way to dial up the kaiju vibes in the neighbourhood even further. Set to commence on 3 November, which coincides with the Japan premiere of the new movie Godzilla-0.0, the melodies are the gift that keeps on giving, as there appears to be no end date for them.

So next time you catch a train at Hibiya, be prepared for the new formidable soundscape that surrounds passengers, and don’t be surprised if you find your eyes drawn to the shadows, searching for a glimpse of Godzilla in the tunnels.

title: Video released of Pikachu’s real-world trip to space! [Video]
description: Face of the Pokémon franchise hitches a ride to the International Space Station as part of European Space Agency mission. Because Pikachu is such an iconic part of the franchise, the Pokémon games and anime have to be careful about introducing new powers for him. Sure, he always needs to be a viable candidate for […]
content:
Face of the Pokémon franchise hitches a ride to the International Space Station as part of European Space Agency mission.

Because Pikachu is such an iconic part of the franchise, the Pokémon games and anime have to be careful about introducing new powers for him. Sure, he always needs to be a viable candidate for whatever adventures are going to take place, but if Pikachu is made too powerful, he loses that quality of being an approachable, believable companion for the protagonist’s journey of growth.

So, ordinarily, Pikachu becoming a Flying-type Pokémon would be going a step too far. The following video showing Pikachu floating in mid-air is no ordinary situation, though, since it was recorded on his real-world trip to the International Space Station!

As revealed last month, a Pikachu plushie accompanied French astronaut Sophie Adenot on her trip to the ISS as part of the European Space Agency’s Epsilon mission. Pikachu even had his own custom-made ESA uniform, complete with a covering for his tail.

In the video, Adenot provides audio commentary for Pikachu’s tour of the ISS’ Nodes 1 and 2. He gets to take a look at the recycled drinking water dispenser, as Adenot explains that 98 percent of the water used on the ISS is recycled, as is its occupants’ urine, though she refrains from revealing whether or not Pikachu was asked to provide his as well. After stopping by the heavy-duty freezers used for experiment sample preservation in the node’s laboratory, Pikachu floats over into the crew quarters section of Node 2, specifically towards the area where astronauts are secured while sleeping, with Adenot hypothesizing that he’s ready for a nap.

▼ Sweet space dreams, Pikachu.

With his trip to the ISS, Pikachu joins the proud tradition of zero-gravity indicators, objects used for visual confirmation that a spacecraft has entered a zero-G environment, and also to demonstrate this status in photos and videos for people back on Earth. Despite their science-y name, zero-gravity indicators are often plushies, but Pikachu appears to the first Pokémon to fill this role.

As the video closes, Adenot mentions that Pikachu will be returning to earth before she does, but he’s still acting as a spokescharacter for the European Space Agency. To coincide with the currently ongoing World Space Week festivities, the Pokémon Center Online is offering a range of Pokémon/ESA crossover merch here, including two different astronaut Pikachu plushies.

title: Shibuya goes hard on Halloween, announces countermeasures to prevent chaos on the streets
description: Tokyo Ward clamps down as this year’s Saturday Halloween poses more dangers than the past six years.  If you’ve ever visited Shibuya’s famous scramble crossing at Halloween, you’ll know how chaotic it can be. Costumes, crowds, street drinking, and people cramming into the crossing and surrounding thoroughfares for photos and impromptu meetups are all the […]
content:
Tokyo Ward clamps down as this year’s Saturday Halloween poses more dangers than the past six years. 

If you’ve ever visited Shibuya’s famous scramble crossing at Halloween, you’ll know how chaotic it can be. Costumes, crowds, street drinking, and people cramming into the crossing and surrounding thoroughfares for photos and impromptu meetups are all the ingredients for mayhem, and after a truck was overturned by revellers in 2018, Shibuya has been doing everything it can to clamp down on the unwanted chaos.

With Halloween falling on a Saturday this year, Shibuya is preparing for more revellers than usual, and is working hard to keep things under control with a new awareness campaign that comes with the slogan “GOODBYE BAD HALLOWEEN”.

The straight-to-the-point, all-caps slogan aims to curb what Shibuya calls “Meiwaku Halloween” (“Nuisance Halloween”) behaviour, which includes drinking and smoking on the street, littering, making excessive noise and obstructing pedestrian traffic while taking photos in costume. Shibuya says this year’s celebrations pose a significatly greater risk as Halloween hasn’t ocurred on a Saturday since 2020, and it estimates that around 18,000 people will be on the streets of Shibuya Center Gai during peak times, compared to 4,200 last year, which was the lowest since records began in 2019, when there were approximately 40,000 visitors.

Though last year’s crowds were thwarted by rain, the decrease in revellers in recent years is all down to Shibuya’s concerted efforts to discourage people from making the scramble crossing area their playground during Halloween. Countermeasures now include a year-round ban on drinking alcohol on the street in Shibuya between 6 p.m. and 5 a.m., introduced in October 2024, and 62 retailers in the vicinity, including convenience stores and department stores, have been asked to refrain from selling alcohol during those hours on Halloween night.

This year also marks the first Halloween since Shibuya began collecting a 2,000-yen (US$13) fine for littering in June, with patrols being increased from the usual three teams of three to five teams of seven on Halloween.

Combined with a large police presence, plus 185 private security guards and 70 ward employees on patrol to curb bad behaviour, Halloween in Shibuya now feels less like a street party and more like a heavily regulated, slightly hostile no-go zone. While this approach has so far been successful in keeping the peace, it does come at a cost, with Shibuya saying it has spent around 74 million yen (about US$468,000) on countermeasures for this year’s Halloween. Of that, around 58 million yen is going towards station-area safety measures, 2 million yen towards rubbish collection and disposal, and 14 million yen towards public-awareness materials like flags and banners.

▼ And, presumably, this awareness video.

Despite all the countermeasures, which include temporary fencing around the famous Hachiko statue to block it from view from 6 a.m. on 30 October until 5 p.m. on 1 November, and the suspension of LUUP and Lime services around Shibuya Station from 5 p.m. on 30 October until 5 a.m. on 31 October, Shibuya Mayor Ken Hasebe isn’t entirely against Halloween.

In speaking to the press, he has been encouraging visitors to enjoy Halloween in Shibuya, just not on the streets, but by attending events organised by shopping streets, commercial facilities and clubs in the ward instead.

So the message from Shibuya this year is clear – the streets are not an all-night party venue. With police and officials out in force during the Halloween weekend, the party vibe of years past is now long gone, so you’d be better off celebrating in other parts of Tokyo instead.

title: Starbucks Japan releases new seasonal chilled cup tea latte with surprising accents in flavour
description: Limited-edition drink serves up a new taste of autumn. Starbucks’ chilled cup range was first released in Japan ahead of the globe over 20 years ago, and since then it’s undergone many transformations, with limited-edition exclusives capturing the taste of the season. Now, as we stride through autumn, the chain is giving us a new […]
content:
Limited-edition drink serves up a new taste of autumn.

Starbucks’ chilled cup range was first released in Japan ahead of the globe over 20 years ago, and since then it’s undergone many transformations, with limited-edition exclusives capturing the taste of the season.

Now, as we stride through autumn, the chain is giving us a new limited-edition release called the Joyful Harmony Tea Latte, which delivers chill autumn vibes with some interesting accents in flavour.

At the heart of the drink is black tea, with oolong and jasmine tea adding extra layers of complexity, combined with a good serving of milk for a creamy finish. The surprise flavour, however, is apricot, which is said to balance well with the fuller body of tea and creamy milk. Though fruity accents tend to act as a mellow counterpart in a lot of teas, Starbucks says this drink has a distinctive rich apricot aroma and a fruity taste reminiscent of perfectly ripe apricots, so you can truly enjoy the taste of the fruit.

The autumn theme is beautifully captured in the design on the cup, which features jasmine flowers, tea leaves and apricots, in gold and warm-toned hues to represent the layers of flavour and fragrance in the beverage.

While the drink can be enjoyed on its own, it’s said to pair particularly well with desserts like Sweet Potato Mont Blanc. According to the chain, the gentle sweetness and smooth texture of this dessert complements the creamy milk and fragrant tea flavours in the latte.

▼ The jasmine aroma and fruity apricot notes enhance the flavour of sweet potato, creating a very autumnal combination.

The chilled cup is a quick and easy way to enjoy Starbucks without having to stop by the chain, and it can be purchased at 7-Eleven stores and other retailers nationwide for a limited time from 13 October, priced at 230 yen (US$1.46).

title: Tokyo government announces removal of all public phones from city’s Toei subway stations
description: Decision wasn’t made by the transportation bureau, though. Generally speaking, when the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Transportation has an announcement to make, it has something to do with trains, buses, or some other form of public transit. One of the organization’s latest statements, though, is about phones. Specifically, it’s about public phones inside subway stations, […]
content:
Decision wasn’t made by the transportation bureau, though.

Generally speaking, when the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Transportation has an announcement to make, it has something to do with trains, buses, or some other form of public transit. One of the organization’s latest statements, though, is about phones. Specifically, it’s about public phones inside subway stations, and how they’re going to be disappearing.

Tokyo is actually big enough that it has two different subway networks. The bureau’s announcement affects the government-managed Toei Subway system, which consists of the Asakusa, Mito, Oedo, and Shinjuku Lines, and the timetable is for none of their stations to have payphone by November of 2028 at the latest.

This isn’t a change that’s being initiated by the Tokyo government, however. Instead, it’s telecommunications operator NTT East that’s saying it wants to remove all of its phones from Toei Subway stations, and the bureau is simply passing on the company’s decision to the general public.

There’s a strong argument to be made that, in this day and age, public phones rarely serve any significant purpose. It’s not unusual for even junior high school kids to have their own smartphones, so pretty much anyone who’s going to be out and about in the city already has a way to make telephone calls, in addition to using messaging and voice chat apps for necessary communication with family, friends, classmates, or colleagues.

▼ Plus you can’t read SoraNews24 on a public phone, and just look at how annoyed this guy is by that shortcoming.

However, pay phones also have a role as disaster-relief infrastructure. Not only can they be used to contact medical and fire services, public phone networks can also be used, for free, in the case of events such as earthquakes and tsunami to make calls and contact voice message services. They provide a critical lifeline for people in disaster-stricken areas whose phones may have been lost or damaged, or who may not have access to a power supply or charging equipment after their phone’s battery runs out.

Because of that, under Japan’s Telecommunications Business Act, licensed payphone providers are required to maintain a certain concentration in areas in which they operate. Specifically, at least one public phone must be installed and in working order for every 500 square meters (5,382 square feet) in urban communities, or one phone for every square kilometer in other areas. These phone, classified as Type-1 Public Phones, should be placed either on public roads or in facilities facing public roads that the general public can access 24 hours a day.

Public phones inside rail stations, however, are not classified as Type-1 Public Phones, most likely because the stations close for several hours at night. Because of that, station phones fall into the category of Type-2 Public Phones, which can be installed or removed at NTT East’s discretion, without any need to obtain permission from the Tokyo government. As such, this appears to be a pure business decision, with NTT East no longer feeling that its in-station phones justify the cost of maintaining them compared to the undoubtedly reduced revenue they bring in.

The phones’ removal is likely to occur gradually over the next two years, and the Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Transportation says that each station will announce its removal date at least two weeks ahead of time. The bureau also recommends that those in need of a payphone utilize the search function on NTT East’s website here, though that, of course, isn’t going to be much help to anyone without a smartphone or other connectable communications device already on them.

title: My Neighbor Totoro calendar for next year can be yours right now at Donguri Kyowakoku
description: Its months don’t start until 2027, but the artwork is adorable and beautiful already. My Neighbor Totoro is unquestionably a classic of animated cinema, and that status is even more impressive when you consider that for almost the entirety of its 86-minute runtime, hardly anything is happening that pushes any sort of narrative forward. content:
Its months don’t start until 2027, but the artwork is adorable and beautiful already.

My Neighbor Totoro is unquestionably a classic of animated cinema, and that status is even more impressive when you consider that for almost the entirety of its 86-minute runtime, hardly anything is happening that pushes any sort of narrative forward. Of course, as fans know, that’s part of the film’s charm. The loose connection from one scene to another helps create a dreamlike plausibility for the anime film’s supernatural elements, and the leisurely pace of what story there is cultivates a permeating sense of nostalgia for the unhurried days of childhood.

Unfortunately, as we grow up and take on adult responsibilities, we have to adhere to more structured schedules than “Go look for forest spirits in the woods, or maybe at the bus stop later if I take a nap first.” But if you want a calendar for keeping track of appointments which will also remind you of the importance of stopping to smell the roses (or other pleasing agrarian aromas), the 2027 Totoro calendar is now available at Studio Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku.

Each page features a scene from the anime, with ample space for writing in your schedule with pen or pencil (Studio Ghibli does love doing things by hand, after all).

There’s even a little bit of linguistics fun to be had, as the artwork for May is taken from the scene where Totoro first meets Mei, whose name is pronounced like “May” (though big sister Satsuki’s name itself means May under the old Japanese naming system for the months of the year).

Official Studio Ghibli merch designers are never ones to skimp on quality, and the calendar’s creators say they made sure to use a paper stock that’s both sturdy and easy to write on, and with a size of 51.5 x 36.4 centimeters (20.3 x 14.3 inches), the illustrations should be large enough to have some visual impact on your home or office.

We’ve still got a few months left to go in 2026, but Donguri Kyowakoku seems to be operating under the sound logic that people who buy calendars are the sort of people who like to plan ahead, and so the calendar is on sale now, priced at 1,980 yen (US$12.50), and can be ordered through the chain’s online store here. Alternatively it remains available through the Ghibli museum shop here.

title: Starbucks Japan unveils new Halloween goods with secret glow-in-the-dark details
description: Tumblers, bottles, Bearistas and cats get us in the mood for spooky season. With Halloween now on the horizon, it’s time to stock up on spooky goods to celebrate the season, and over at Starbucks there’s a bevvy of goods to bring a dash of scary cuteness to your beverages. content:
Tumblers, bottles, Bearistas and cats get us in the mood for spooky season.

With Halloween now on the horizon, it’s time to stock up on spooky goods to celebrate the season, and over at Starbucks there’s a bevvy of goods to bring a dash of scary cuteness to your beverages.

Designed around the concept of “Moon Light Halloween“, the new collection covers a wide array of drink bottles and tumblers, with sparkles, shimmers, and glow-in-the-dark details conjuring up the mysterious beauty of a moonlit evening. With over a dozen items to choose from, there’s something to suit all types of Starbucks lovers, particularly those with a soft spot for cats, as felines feature prominently in the range.

▼ Stainless Steel To-Go Bottle – Cat Light Pink, 473 millilitres (5,500 yen [US$34.78])

This bottle serves up cute cat details on the front, where a white feline sits beneath a starry sky, and on the back, where you’ll find cat-shaped customisation boxes, with a single moon thrown in.

▼ The push-button unlock feature means you won’t have to worry about spills.

▼ Stainless Steel Bottle – Glitter Light Purple, 444 millilitres (4,900 yen)

This beautiful bottle has a glittery surface that sparkles in the light, and a subdued celestial cat design for refined elegance.

▼ Stainless Steel Logo Bottle – Cat Glow in the Dark, 473 millilitres (4,950 yen)

Venture into the darkness of the night with this jet-black bottle, which cleverly incorporates black cats into the design, alongside one solitary white feline.

▼ Switch off the lights and the white cat glows in the dark, thanks to its phosphorescent coating.

▼ Stainless Steel Cold Cup Tumbler – Glitter Pink, 591 millilitres (5,450 yen)

This showstopper of a tumbler shimmers with a hot pink glittery surface, offset by cat-and-moon customisation boxes on the rear…

▼ …and a very cute straw cap that depicts a black cat sitting on the moon.

▼ Snow Globe Tumbler – Cat Glow in the Dark 355 millilitres (3,400 yen)

This tumbler looks set to be a sell-out hit, with the snow globe feature in the base containing a black cat, paw raised as if playing with the stars that swirl around it.

▼ To make things even cuter, the stars around the body of the bottle glow in the dark.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler – Cat 473 millilitres (2,800 yen)

Sip from between a cat’s ears with this sweet tumbler, which changes colour from light to dark pink with the addition of cold water.

▼ Double Wall Heat-Resistant Glass Cup – Cat Glow in the Dark 355 millilitres (3,700 yen)

▼ This glass cup also lets you drink from a cat, thanks to the adorable cat-ear lid.

The clever design gives the black cat a set of devilish bat-like wings, and when the lights are out, the scene comes to life with glow-in-the-dark confetti scattering and sparkling with every movement of the glass.

▼ Coaster – Cat (2,200 yen)

This cute coaster is as practical as it is beautiful, with its hot pink hue catching the eye, and moon-and-star details setting the scene for our black cat and cat bat.

▼ The perfect coaster for the Glass Cup.

▼ Colour-Changing Reusable Cup 473 millilitres (700 yen)

▼ This affordable cup changes colour when you pour a hot drink into it, transforming the black cat into…

▼ … a white cat!

▼ Colour-Changing Reusable Cup 473 millilitres + Reusable Cup Exclusive Drink Hole Cap Bearista Cat (1,350 yen)

Add on a cute Bearista cap and your drink will be less prone to spilling and more prone to compliments.

▼ Bearista Mini (2,750 yen)

The chain’s beloved Bearista character slips into a black cat costume for Halloween, and will look very cute when clipped onto a bag or keychain.

▼ Starbucks Mini Cup Gift with drink ticket (1,150 yen)

Those wanting to share the love have several options to choose from, with the Mini Cup Gift being arguably the cutest.

You can mimic the colour-changing effect of the larger Cold Cup Tumbler by slipping the hot pink insert in and out of the cup.

The tiny size lets you store small items like paper clips, so you can enjoy the beauty of the cup while it serves a practical purpose as part of your stationery collection.

▼ Bearista Message Gift with drink ticket (1,650 yen)

▼ For a message with soft and cuddly feels, this gift set ticks all the boxes.

It contains a drink ticket, up to the value of 700 yen for dine-in orders or 687 yen to-go, with a section where you can write a message to the recipient.

There’s also a bag for gifting, which neatly holds the card and the Bearista in batwing costume.

▼ Beverage Card with drink ticket (750 yen)

Finally, we have a shiny drink ticket, which opens up like a card for you to write a message on.

Well, that was a lovely walk in the moonlight, and now we’re definitely in the mood for Halloween. As always, the products are available for a limited time, from 9 October, and they’ll be available at Starbucks stores around Japan and online, while stocks last.

content:
The Phantom Purple Cat brings mysterious charm to two exclusive limited-edition drinks.

Now that we’re in October, Halloween is right around the corner, and Starbucks is here to celebrate with a playful new limited-edition Frappuccino inspired by a phantom cat.

The feline, known as the “Phantom Purple Cat”, sits at the centre of this year’s Starbucks celebrations, with the theme being “Halloween Purple Cat in Mystery Forest” (yes, that’s the exact official English rendering).

The elusive cat is ready to lure customers into the forest with the new limited-edition Blackberry Yogurt Frappuccino, which comes in two varieties.

▼ Black Ears Version and White Ears Version.

Common to both drinks is a fruity blueberry yogurt base, which has a sharp yet pleasant acidity and a soft, fruit-like texture. Blackberry chocolate sauce adds a deep accent in colour and flavour, and both drinks are finished with a chocolate topper shaped like cat ears, to make it seem as if the phantom cat is peeking out of the cup.

▼ The Black Ears Version uses bitter chocolate for a cooler, more grown-up look and flavour…

▼ … while the White Ears Version has a sweeter, milkier taste and a cuter look.

You can choose your cat to match your mood, but whichever feline you choose, the purple kitty will be close by watching from the sidelines, with Starbucks saying it will be hiding quietly around stores.

▼ Customers can find the purple cat by following its in-store footprints.

Joining the felines for a limited time is a special limited-edition sweet, with its dark hues and green filling matching the mood of the mystery forest.

▼ Matcha Anko Butter Chocolate Scone Sandwich

According to Starbucks, this scone resembles “a ghost sticking out its tongue“, and it contains a well-balanced sweetness, saltiness, and bitterness that pairs well with the drinks.

As an added bonus, Starbucks Rewards members who purchase one of the cat-eared Frappuccinos will be able to receive a free chocolate chips customisation by using the app or presenting the designated QR code at the register from 9-15 October.

Both drinks will be available in a Tall size only, priced at 730 yen (US$4.60) for dine-in or 717 yen for takeout. They’ll be on the menu for a limited time from 9 October.

content:
Sometimes Japanese portion sizes are small… and sometimes they look like this.

Wendy’s is often overlooked in Japan, but right now it’s towering over the competition with a new burger called MEGA Wendy’s. The all-caps in the name is certainly warranted, because it’s even bigger than the three-patty Wendy’s Burger USA Triple (known as “Dave’s Single” in the U.S.), with four extra beef patties and four slices of cheese giving it a total of seven patties and an astonishing 2,614 kilocalories.

Our reporter Kouhey has taken on all kinds of big burger challenges over the years, but this one looked so formidable that he spent a long time wondering whether he should even take it on. However, after finding out that the new burger was released nationwide to commemorate its appearance on TV, he realised he may never get the chance to take on such a heavyweight again, so he shrugged off his concerns and headed out to his nearest branch.

After arriving at the Iidabashi Ramla store, located in the Iidabashi Ramla commercial complex next to JR Iidabashi Station, he walked over to one of the self-service kiosks and blinked in surprised when he saw the burger on the menu, branded with a “New Product” tag and standing there like a meat tower.

▼ His eyes widened further when he saw the price – the burger, on its own, was a whopping 3,670 yen (US$23.36).

This was the first time he’d seen a burger this expensive at a chain restaurant, and it was so pricey that he had to check whether he had enough in his wallet to cover it. Fortunately, he did, so he ordered it as part of a drink set, bringing the total to 3,910 yen.

Looking at the stats, the MEGA Wendy’s is approximately 14 centimetres (5.5 inches) tall and weighs 900 grams (1.98 pounds). This was way bigger than Burger King’s four-patty Crown The One Pounder, which Kouhey previously battled with in 2023, so he felt slightly wary of this new opponent, which was in a totally different weight class.

After about five minutes of waiting, Kouhey’s number was called, and when he took the tray over to his table, he felt his muscles activate under the weight of the tray.

▼ “What the heck is this?!” He thought to himself. “Is it an iron ball?”

Even while wrapped in its paper, the burger was already a massive round mass. Looking closely, he could see the words “CHICKEN” and “SPECIAL” printed on the paper, and it was so large that it had been wrapped around the burger several times.

▼ Picking it up, it was seriously heavy – like something you could use for strength training.

Carefully unpeeling the wrap… the monster revealed itself.

▼ Meat, meat, meat, meat, meat, meat, meat!!!

It truly was a wall of meat. Seven patties were stacked up on top of each other, pushing the top bun upwards. When he lifted the bun, he could see onions, ketchup and lettuce sitting above it all, giving it the character of a burger, but with a mountain of meat underneath.

Looking closely, Kouhey discovered a good amount of cheddar cheese between the patties, and when he gently pried them apart, the melted cheese looked nice and gooey.

Though all the components of a good burger were clearly present, Kouhey was surprised at how the buns seemed so miniscule – the top and bottom buns were completely outdone by the seven patties between them.

▼ Then there was the burger packaging, which was enormous when he spread it out, giving you an idea of just how big the burger was.

At 14 centimetres tall, this is a seriously tall burger, and it was a tall order to eat. As the battle between man and burger began, Kouhey, gripped the burger firmly and brought it up to his mouth…

▼ …but the thing was so huge that he could only eat the meat.

No matter how much he ate, every mouthful consisted of nothing but meat, and sometimes a little cheese. Every now and then, a hint of bun or a skerrick of onion would timidly make its way into the mix, but it felt less like eating a hamburger and more like eating a lump of meat with cheese sandwiched in between.

About halfway through, he took a breather and paused to check the cross-section.

▼ There was still a lot left.

As a seasoned big burger professional, Kouhey knew he was now entering the “flavour-change zone”. This is what he likes to call the stage where your palate gets so tired of the monotonous flavours that you need to add a little something extra to keep you going until the end, and to help with his, he added some habanero sauce, which he’d picked up from beside the register.

Drizzling it over the cross-section of the patties, he wondered what kind of difference the sauce would make to the flavour profile.

▼ Whoah. This was actually good.

The spiciness and acidity enlivened his palate, lifting it from all the meat and cheese that had been weighing it down. After the endless procession of meat, the sauce provided some welcome relief, helping him through the second half. Although the meat remained the star of the show, there was no stopping Kouhey’s momentum now, so it didn’t take long for the tower, which had once seemed impossibly tall, to shrink down to a size that fit in the palm of his hand.

▼ A few more bites and finally, the end came into view.

▼ Then, the final bite.

▼ K.O.!

With his belly now full, Kouhey let a smile drift across his face as he reveled in his sense of achievement at having devoured the beast. Looking back at the timestamps on his photos, he found that it’d taken about 18 minutes between him receiving the tray and folding away the burger wrap at the very end of the meal. Although he had to stop repeatedly to take photos, he’d completed the task in good time, and he could confidently say this is the most amount of meat he’s ever eaten in a single sitting.

In the end, the MEGA Wendy’s was less a hamburger and more of a meat-eating challenge. If you feel ready to take on the challenge, be sure to stop by Wendy’s soon as it’s only a limited-time menu item, and come prepared with an empty stomach to take on the beast.

title: Tokyo no-map-app walk! Getting lost with Mr. Sato on the way to Kishimojin
description: Mr. Sato wanted to get lost in order to rediscover the joy of urban exploring. With the wonders of modern technology, there’s hardly any fear of getting lost when you’re out and about. Unfortunately, that also means there’s hardly any hope of getting lost either. This is the dilemma that our ace reporter Mr. Sato […]
content:
Mr. Sato wanted to get lost in order to rediscover the joy of urban exploring.

With the wonders of modern technology, there’s hardly any fear of getting lost when you’re out and about. Unfortunately, that also means there’s hardly any hope of getting lost either.

This is the dilemma that our ace reporter Mr. Sato has been faced with recently. Plugging your destination into the smartphone map app of your choice will pretty much guarantee you can get to where you want to go without any problems. You’ll probably also get there without any discoveries or sense of adventure, and you also might not develop much of a sense of the actual geography when you’re relying on your screen rather than your sense of spatial awareness and observation of your physical surroundings to figure out which way you need to go.

All of this recently has Mr. Sato thinking:

“I want to get lost.”

Of course, it would be irresponsible for us to blindfold Mr. Sato, drive him up into the mountains, drop him off on a random forest road, and say “Have fun finding your way home!” Entertaining…but still irresponsible. So instead, Mr. Sato decided to see if he could find his way to Kishimojn, a temple in Tokyo’s Zoshigaya neighborhood, without using any online maps or navigation apps.

The only bit of online preplanning Mr. Sato allowed himself was to check the closest train station to the temple, which turned out to be Mejiro Station on the Yamanote Line. With that confirmed, he set his phone to focus mode to disable maps, and headed out of his apartment.

His first stop was Nakano Station, the closest rail stop to his home. Since Mr. Sato had never been to the part of Tokyo he was headed to, he wasn’t sure exactly how to get to Mejiro Station. Since this was to be a no-smartphone run, he had to check the board posted above Nakano Station’s ticket machines, something he hasn’t done in ages.

Searching through the web of crisscrossing lines, he was happy to find that it’s a pretty simple route from Nakano (中野) to Mejiro (目白), with just a single transfer at Shinjuku (新宿).

After about 20 minutes on the train, Mr. Sato arrived at Mejiro Station.

Like most stations in downtown Tokyo, Mejiro Station has a map near the ticket gates with local points of interested marked on it. Kishimojn isn’t super famous, but the temple is still a local landmark, so Mr. Sato figured it’d be easy to spot…

…but after sweeping his eyes over the map several times, he still didn’t see it.

Luckily, there was another place he could turn to for help: the koban, or police box, right next to the station.

Koban are like little satellite police stations, but with Japan’s low crime rate, there’s usually quite a bit of downtime for the officers on duty, and they’re generally happy to help with directions. Mr. Sato asked if they could tell him how to get to Kishimojin, and a friendly, courteous officer told him to turn to his right when he exited the koban, follow Mejiro-dori (the street that runs in front of the station) until he crossed a bridge and got to a police station on the far side, and then ask again there.

Mr. Sato said thank you to the officers, and then he was on his way! Heading east on Mejiro-dori, in just a few minutes his steps carried him past the gate of Gakushuin, one of Japan’s most prestigious private universities.

After walking for a few more minutes, he spotted a tall building in the distance that looked like a police station to him. In order to take a more direct path to it, he veered off of Mejiro-dori, figuring that since the police officer had told him to get the final directions to the temple there, he’d probably only have to make one more turn to get to Kishimojin.

Heck, maybe he wouldn’t even have to ask for directions again. By this point, he was probably close enough that he’d start seeing signs on the street pointing the way to the temple, right?

…right…?

Not only did Mr. Sato not see any signs for the temple, he could no longer see the building he’d thought was the police station, a building that, it should be emphasized, he did not know for sure actually was the police station.

In other words…

…Mr. Sato was lost!

So, hey, mission accomplished, right? Well, only half-accomplished so far, because Mr. Sato’s objective was to get lost and make his way to Kishimojin, so now he needed to get his bearings and figure out how to correct his course.

Thankfully, Mr. Sato did at least have a sense that the temple is located near the tracks of the Arakawa Line, and he could see a rail overpass up ahead of him.

So if he more or less followed the tracks, he should eventually make it to Kishimojin, right?

There was, however, a critical flaw in this plan. See, the Arakawa Line is a quaint streetcar line, but what came zooming by on the tracks Mr. Sato was following was a regular, full-size commuter train.

As a matter of fact, this was a Tobu Railway carriage, meaning that this line was actually headed to Ikebukuro Station, and that Mr. Sato had somehow wound up pretty far to the north of Mejiro Station since he started walking, rather than making his way east towards Kishimojin.

▼ The start of the Ikebukuro department store/shopping district

So Mr. Sato turned around and started heading back towards the way he came, trying to find some sign of the Zoshigaya neighborhood that temple is located in. He felt a sense of relief when he spotted a walkway with Zoshigaya Pedestrian Overpass (雑司ヶ谷歩道橋) written on it, and got even more excited when he looked beyond it and saw a sidestreet with an archway with the characters for sando (参道), meaning the approach to a temple or shrine!

This turned out to be the approach to Otori Shrine (大鳥神社), though, not Kishimojin

However, passing underneath the bridge and continuing one block further down the road brought Mr. Sato to the Kishimojin Nishi Sando (鬼子母神西参道), or west-side approach to Kishimojin!

Mr. Sato had been expecting to reach the temple by its east-side approach, since that path runs closer to Mejiro-dori. Because he’d gotten turned around and wandered so much farther north than he’d planned on, and since the Nishi Sando runs to the northwest from Kishimojin, that’s the road by which he ended up finally getting to his destination.

As noted above, Kishimojin is written in Japanese as 鬼子母神, and those characters translate to “demon,” “child,” “mother,” and “god.” According to Buddhist lore, Kishimojin was a demon who would abduct innocent children to feed to her own offspring. Eventually shown the error of her ways, Kishimojin repented and reformed, becoming a deity of protection for children and expectant mothers, and it remains a popular place for pregnant women and their well-wishing friends and family members to visit.

If you take the direct route from Mejiro Station to Kishimojin, it’s about a 12-minute walk. Mr. Sato’s ambling course, on the other hand, took about an hour to complete. He had no complaints, though, since that sense of exploration and mental mapping had been exactly the sort of stimulation he’d been craving. With his quest completed, he felt the sort of satisfaction that comes from completing a fun but challenging puzzle or video game.

Speaking of mental mapping, after leaving the temple Mr. Sato strolled east for a bit, and that’s where he finally reached the tracks of the Arakawa Line, and also the Zoshigaya subway station (which doesn’t have any lines that he could take home to Nakano).

So how did Mr. Sato end up getting lost in the first place? You might have already put the pieces together, but let’s go back and review the directions Mr. Sato got at the police box.

Mr. Sato asked if they could tell him how to get to Kishimojin, and a friendly, courteous officer told him to turn to his right when he exited the koban, follow Mejiro-dori (the street that runs in front of the station) until he crossed a bridge and got to a police station on the far side, and then ask again there.

But wait, we never mentioned Mr. Sato crossing over a bridge, did we? Nope…because he never did. He turned off of Mejiro-dori much earlier than he was supposed to, which is why he ended up making it all the way to the edge of Ikebukuro without realizing how off course he was.

Now armed with the clearer sense of geography that came from having relied on his brain, not an app, to navigate, Mr. Sato was able to find his way back to Mejiro Station with no problems at all.

▼ He even got to cross over the bridge he was supposed to.

Oh, and the part earlier about Mr. Sato not seeing Kishimojin on the map at Mejiro Station?

Yeah…

…it turns out Kishimojin (鬼子母神) actually is marked on the map. Mr. Sato just didn’t notice it.

But again, getting lost was part of what Mr. Sato was hoping for, and he had such a good time that he’s hoping to get lost again soon. So say hi if you happen to run into him on the street in Tokyo, and maybe point him in the direction of home if he needs help.

title: Yogurt and Japanese koji fungus is Japan’s latest food trend, but how does it taste? [Taste test]
description: “Hey dude, put some fungus on this!” isn’t an ordinary food hack, but koji is no ordinary fungus. A lot of people like to mix a little something into their yogurt to give it some extra flavor, like chopped fruit, sliced nuts, or jam. Today, though, we’re recommending that you enhance your yogurt by adding […]
content:
“Hey dude, put some fungus on this!” isn’t an ordinary food hack, but koji is no ordinary fungus.

A lot of people like to mix a little something into their yogurt to give it some extra flavor, like chopped fruit, sliced nuts, or jam. Today, though, we’re recommending that you enhance your yogurt by adding fungus.

Hey, wait! Where are you going? Was it something we said? It…it was the fungus, wasn’t it?

Just hear us out, though. We’re not talking about any old fungus. We’re talking about koji, an edible, non-harmful culture that can be cultivated to grow on rice. As a matter of fact, you already have some first-hand koji experience if you’ve eaten miso or drunk sake, since koji is a key ingredient in their production.

So with that out of the way, let’s take a look at one of Japan’s new food hack trends, adding shio koji/salted koji to yogurt, then draining off the water, which fans say creates a uniquely delicious flavor.

▼ Shio koji

Shio koji can be purchased in Japanese markets and specialty shops, as well as online (Amazon Japan has several varieties here). The recommended ratio is one or two tablespoons of shio koji per 400 grams (14.1 ounces) of yogurt, so we went with 1.5 tablespoons.

▼ Spooning the shio koji into the yogurt container

After stirring the yogurt and shio koji together, all that was left to do was put the mixture into a yogurt strainer, and put the strainer into the fridge while the excess liquid dripped off.

Though our strainer bills itself as “quick,” we wanted a nicely firm texture for our shio koji yogurt, so we let it strain for two days. When we took the strainer back out of the fridge and scooped its contents into a bowl, it had a smooth, creamy texture almost exactly like cream cheese.

And it tasted quite a bit like cream cheese too! The added saltiness of the shio koji almost completely mellowed out the sour notes in the yogurt’s flavor profile, leaving us with an enticing creaminess and smooth finish.

We could have happily eaten the whole batch as-is with a spoon, but in order to conduct more thorough testing we grabbed a box of Ritz crackers and spread some shio koji yogurt on top, which we then confirmed to be a very tasty combination.

Finally, we tried drizzling some honey on top, which completely removed any remaining sourness and left us with an invigoratingly salty-sweet finish instead.

So whether you’re looking for a way to spruce up your yogurt or a healthy alternative to cream cheese, it turns out that yogurt and shio koji are indeed a match worth making in your refrigerator.

title: Nissin takes the lid off its first-ever Cup Noodle Point Program for you to win fun prizes

content:
The more noodles you slurp up, the more kinds of instant noodle-themed prizes you can enter to win.

Nissin Foods is celebrating 55 years of its iconic Cup Noodle brand with the first-of-its-kind permanent Cup Noodle Point Program, in which you can enter to win fun prizes ranging from Cup Noodle’s Mystery Meat-themed functional decor to a full day of fun with a friend at Universal Studios Japan.

Residents of Japan are eligible for the program where you earn 1 point per Cup Noodle brand item bought. Most standard-sized Cup Noodle products qualify, though you can always double check the packaging to make sure it displays the point program’s information and a sample QR code, as shown below.

▼ Eligible Cup Noodle Point Program products will display a small QR code for easy recognition.

To participate, just create a new account (you can pre-register using the QR code here) and scan the QR code found after you’ve purchased and opened an eligible product. Your member rank will go up as you accumulate more and more points, as will the variety of the rewards that you can apply for. The current ranks–with whimsical designs of the Mystery Meat character mascot to match–are as follows:

● Mini: 1-4 points
● Regular: 5-9 points
● Big: 10-19 points
● King: 20-49 points
● Mega: 50+ points

▼ Cup Noodle Point Program member ranks

All participants can download a free present of Cup Noodle-themed smartphone wallpaper. Otherwise, there are two methods for entering to win prizes via a time-based system and via a lottery system.

The time-based system is perfect for those who love a first-come, first-served challenge when the clock resets every week on Mondays at 7:30 p.m. JST. Each of the below rewards is limited to a different number of winners per week, ranging from 10 to 100, depending on the prize.

● [100 winners] Cup Noodle ingredients character stickers (set of four)
● [40 winners] Cup Noodle “The Fork” (right-handed or left-handed versions)
● [100 winners] Cup Noodle-shaped reusable bags (random from three designs)
● [50 winners] Cup Noodle ingredients character keychain
● [10 winners] Cup Noodle bento box
● [10 winners] Cup Noodle rug mat

Meanwhile, the lottery-based system contains some unexpectedly fun brand tie-in prizes that you can enter to win by using a specified number of points. You must have Big Rank or above to enter.

● [3 points] Cup Noodle x Bandai Gashapon logo accessory (random from six designs)
● [3 points] Cup Noodle x Clubhaus golf ball marker (red, yellow, blue, green)
● [5 points] Cup Noodle x Clubhaus Fairway Wood headcover (red, yellow, blue, green)
● [5 points] Cup Noodle x Columbia Basin to Garden short sleeve t-shirt in large size (white and black colors)
● [7 points] Cup Noodle Mystery Meat ottoman
● [8 points] Cup Noodle mahjong tiles
● [30 points] A full day of fun at Universal Studios Japan with a party and private night rental (for two people)

▼ Time-based prizes (first six pictured below) and lottery-based prizes (last seven pictured below)

If you’re confused about that last one, it turns out that Nissin Foods is an official marketing partner of Universal Studios Japan–something that we certainly won’t complain about!

The possible rewards will likely continue to grow and evolve over time, so check back on the official website frequently for any updates. It’s also important to note that on your one-year anniversary of registering for the Cup Noodle Point Program, any unused points you’ve accumulated will expire, but on the second-year anniversary and beyond, your member rank will remain the same as the rank you ended on in the previous year.

On our end, we’ll start accumulating points to try to score one of the above prizes ASAP. At the very least, it sounds like a great opportunity to try out more slightly unhinged Cup Noodle recipe ideas as well.

content:
Having a big baby may be decidedly not fun for the mother, the baby’s first bank account will positively rejoice!

Beginning on October 1, babies in Miyagi Prefecture can receive celebratory money for being born–and the bigger the baby, the more the money.

Sendai Bank will deposit the equivalent number of yen as the child’s weight in grams at birth upon creation of the first bank account in their name if certain requirements are met. For instance, a baby born at 3,250 grams (7.17 pounds) will receive a gift of 3,250 yen (US$20.59) in their account. The idea was actually devised by an employee, and the bank hopes that this new perk will encourage families to use their services for a long time as the child grows older.

▼ The monetary gift can also be used to help offset the costs of new babies accidentally damaging their parents’ devices.

The main eligibility requirements are that the child is six years or under and received a Sukusuku (“healthy growing”) Box, which is a project being implemented as child-rearing assistance throughout Miyagi Prefecture. The box is filled with helpful childcare items and samples from sponsoring companies. In addition, parents must also deposit a minimum of 30,000 yen into the new bank account at the time of its creation.

For anyone wondering, no, you can’t simply fudge the numbers to make it appear that your baby was born extra chubby. Sendai Bank will confirm the baby’s weight at the time of birth via the official Maternal and Child Health Handbook, a helpful log and guidebook distributed by municipalities that tracks a baby’s growth during pregnancy and post-partum by healthcare professionals. Still, though, if you’re expecting a little one soon, it wouldn’t hurt to try eating some big food before birth to wish for a big bank account.

title: Osaka man arrested for running little pet shop of horrors with dangerous crocodile
description: Your one-stop shop for abused deadly animals. It seems like pet store regulations in Japan tend to be on the lax side. The other day, while taking my daughter through a major home center’s pet section, among the puppies and parrots, I saw a meerkat for sale. What the heck is someone going to do […]
content:
Your one-stop shop for abused deadly animals.

It seems like pet store regulations in Japan tend to be on the lax side. The other day, while taking my daughter through a major home center’s pet section, among the puppies and parrots, I saw a meerkat for sale. What the heck is someone going to do with a meerkat? Are they going to buy some Meerkat Chow at the supermarket?

So, to be a pet store with an illegal collection of animals in Japan, it seems like you have to really put in the effort to lower the bar. That’s just what one resident of Higashiyodogawa Ward in Osaka City had been doing before police finally put a stop to it.

Soma Satomi, the proprietor of a pet shop in the area, was arrested for violating the Act on Welfare and Management of Animals as well as other regulations, after animals such as 21 snapping turtles and a 1.5-meter (5-foot) saltwater crocodile were discovered by police in the store’s back area. In the main area, other exotic animals like bats and scorpions were sold.

The snapping turtles are designated as Specified Invasive Alien Species for the ecological threat they pose in Japan, while the crocodile is a Specified Animal, meaning it poses a potential risk to human life. The crocodile was not yet fully grown, but this species, which has been known to attack humans, is capable of growing to over four meters (13 feet) in length.

▼ A news report about the arrest

The 34-year-old’s pet shop itself hardly seemed up to code either. In fact, when reporters spoke with local residents, very few of them even knew the building sold pets. In addition, the crocodile inside was being kept in an acrylic tank that Satomi appeared to have built himself, measuring only slightly larger than the croc itself at, 150 centimeters long by 61 centimeters high (59 by 24 inches). It was secured by putting a wire mesh over the top of the tank and placing something heavy on top of that.

▼ The location of the pet store. It appears to have been a skateboard shop when this Google Street View images was taken a year ago, but it gives a good sense of how populated the area is.

According to Satomi, the crocodile was his personal pet, and not for sale. That didn’t win him affection from anyone, according to online comments about the news, many of which shuddered to think what could have happened if the animals had escaped.

“I love reptiles, but that is not the behavior of someone who loves reptiles.”
“What was he going to do when he couldn’t take care of them? Abandon them somewhere?”
“Just outlaw pet shops!”
“About 30 years ago, I heard that someone was keeping a cheetah or a leopard at a house near my home. I thought it was a joke, but when I went to see, there really was one pacing around in a wire cage.”
“I once saw this crocodile named Hook at Ueno Zoo during feeding time and was shocked at how high those things can jump.”
“Japan makes it too easy to import wild animals, and the situation allows amateurs to buy and keep them with virtually no oversight.”
“Imagine the flooding Japan’s been experiencing this year happens there. That crocodile would have the run of the town.”

It’s probably safe to say the not-so-unlikely event of a flood occurring and allowing this amphibious apex predator its long-awaited freedom never occurred to its owner. After all, anyone who decided to keep a potentially massive dangerous animal with a lifespan rivaling their own as a pet isn’t especially gifted in foresight.

Hopefully, this particular croc will get a nice, spacious enclosure at a zoo somewhere, where it has all the room it needs to… Well, I guess they do just sit there most of the time, but at least it will have the option of moving around, and that’s what counts.

title: Krispy Kreme Japan gets extra-local with adorable new Hokkaido snow fairy donuts
description: Northern Japan’s heart-meltingly cute birds inspire new mouthwatering sweets. A lot of foreign sweets brands that set up shops in Japan create special desserts that cater to local Japanese tastes, and things get even more focused for Krispy Kreme with its Premium Hokkaido series. These donuts draw inspiration from Japan’s northernmost prefecture featuring not only […]
content:
Northern Japan’s heart-meltingly cute birds inspire new mouthwatering sweets.

A lot of foreign sweets brands that set up shops in Japan create special desserts that cater to local Japanese tastes, and things get even more focused for Krispy Kreme with its Premium Hokkaido series. These donuts draw inspiration from Japan’s northernmost prefecture featuring not only ingredients sourced from Hokkaido, but which also act as sweet little salutes to the region’s culture and scenery.

So as of October 7, while you can get your sweets fix with one of Krispy Kreme’s original glazed donuts, you can also satisfy your cravings with the adorable new Premium Hokkaido Milky White Shimaenaga.

“What’s Shimaenaga?” and “What’s that thing in the middle of the donut?” are two questions you might be asking, and their answers overlap. The shimaenaga/shima enaga is a species of small bird (roughly 12 centimeters [4.7 inches] in length) that lives in Hokkaido. In winter, their white feathers puff up to help insulate them from the cold, making them look like fluffy little snowballs, and their overall adorableness has earned them the nickname of “snow fairies.”

▼ Shima enaga

The shima enaga, commonly known in English as the long-tailed tit, is a beloved symbol of Hokkaido, and so peeking out from the center of the Premium Hokkaido Milky White Shimaenaga is a snow fairy rendered in milky cream sourced from Hokkaido dairies, with a pair of amanatto (candied red beans) for wings and dots of chocolate for its eyes and beak. The donut itself, meanwhile, has a milky white chocolate coating sprinkled with crunchy bits of white chocolate and silver dragées, evoking thoughts of a glittering Hokkaido winter snowscape.

The Milky White Shimaenaga marks the third time for the snow fairy to be Krispy Kreme Japan’s muse, but this specific combination of flavors is being offered for the first time. As is the norm for the Premium Hokkaido line, it’s exclusive to select Krispy Kreme locations in Hokkaido, specifically the Sitatte Sapporo, Sapporo Pole Town, Sapporo Le Trois, Chitose Outlet Mall Rera, and Mitsui Outlet Park Sapporo Kitahiroshima branches. It’s scheduled to be available from October 7 through late April, and while Hokkaido is a little outside our usual snack run radius, delicious donuts sound like a perfectly good reason to take a trip into Japan’s north.

content:
Why build a bear when you could build a Totoro?

I don’t think it’s really going out on a limb to speculate that “people who want to visit Japan’s Studio Ghibli anime theme park” and “people who want to hug Totoro” are two groups with a whole lot of overlap. I’m not saying the Venn diagram of those two demographics is a single, perfect circle, but it’s got to be pretty close, right?

While we’re at it, we can probably say that a lot of people in those largely identical groups would also like to make their own Totoro plushie, and it just so happens that that’s something visitors to the Ghibli Park park in Aichi Prefecture will be able to do next month.

And no, “Ghibli Park park” isn’t a typo. Instead of being a single self-contained facility, Ghibli Park is made up of a number of detached sections which are all within Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, in the town of Nagakute (near Nagoya). The upcoming Let’s Make a One-of-a-Kind Totoro Plushie workshop is being promoted by Ghibli Park, but is actually being held at the Chikyu Shimin Koryu Center community center, which is also located in Aichi Commemorative Park, just a little north of Ghibli Park’s Hill of Youth area and to the west of the Valley of Witches.

▼ Chikyu Shimin Koryu Center

In the 70-minute workshop, which is open to participants ages 6 and up, you’ll attach your Totoro plushie’s eyes, give him an accessory leaf, stuff him with cotton, sew up the seam along his back, and then be able to take him home to hug at your leisure (or, more likely, begin immediately hugging right there in the park).

Because the workshop isn’t being held within Ghibli Park itself, Ghibli Park tickets aren’t required. However, demand is sure to be high for the total of eight sessions held across two days (10 a.m. and 12:40, 2:20, and 4 p.m. on November 21 and 22), so reservations are being done via an online lottery system administered by Boo-Woo Ticket, the same ticketing service that handles tickets for Ghibli Park. Applications will be open from October 7 to 12, with winners to be notified on the evening of October 16. Up to two reservations can be made per applicant, with a per-person participation/materials fee of 7,000 yen (US$44).

Because the workshops are capped at 32 people, it’s going to take some luck to snag a spot. However, if you aren’t able to take part in the Aichi Commemorative Park sessions, you can take heart in knowing that they’re actually a special traveling itinerary of a regularly held make-your-own-Totoro-plushie event at the Izy Teddy Bear Museum in Shizuoka Prefecture and Nasu Teddy Bear Museum in Tochigi Prefecture.

▼ According to their website, the Izu teddy Bear Museum even lets you make Catbus plushies!

However, making your on Totoro plushie just after or before visiting Ghibli Park does sound like it’d make the experience extra special, and you can find the Aichi event’s reservation application page here.

title: Viral Yokohama cafe tops teas with mini teapots with a clever smoldering secret [Photos]
description: We head to Chazhong for a treat for our taste buds and our eyes. content:
We head to Chazhong for a treat for our taste buds and our eyes.

Japan loves all manner of tasty things, but stuff that tastes good and looks good earns a special place in people’s hearts. That presents a special challenge, though, for drink makers, since while a cafe can make its taiyaki fish-shaped cakes surf on waves of ice cream or bake cream puffs that look like Totoro, there’s not much you can do to creatively shape or position liquid refreshment.

But one cafe in Yokohama has been serving up smiles with its beverages, since the cups that its teas come in are topped with little teapots of their own.

The cafe, which opened in Yokohama’s Chinatown this past summer and quickly started generating buzz online, is called Chazhong. Since it’s only about a half-hour from downtown Tokyo to Yokohama, we hopped on the train and rode until Motomachi Chukaigai Station, then took the five-minute stroll over to Koi Koi Yokocho, the food hall that Chazhong is located inside of.

Chazhong has a menu made of up of milk teas using various kinds of Chinese teas, including oolong, white, and pu’er teas, as their base.

That already gives the place a pretty unique concept, but what really makes the place special is that when you purchase your drink ticket from the cafe’s machine, you not only select the size, amount of sugar, and whether you want your tea hot or cold, you also pick between a brown or red teapot…

…which sits on top of your cup’s lid.

That’s not any sort of CG or edited-in visual effect, either. There actually is a wisp of smoke or steam that rises out of the pot.

How does Chazhong pull off this cool trick? At first we thought the teapot might be open at the bottom, and steam was just rising up from the tea that’s inside the paper cup, but that’s not the case.

But the tiny teapot isn’t filled with boiling liquid of its own that steam is rising from either, since it’s too small to heat up on a stove.

However, it turns out there is water inside the pot, plus one other key component: dry ice. That combination produces a whisp of rising smoke that lasts for about 2 minutes, long enough to let you snap some very cook pictures, but not so long that you’ll have to worry about brushing it away while you’re actually drinking your tea,

As for the tea itself, our taste-testing reporter Yayoi Saginomiya’s hot, unsweetened Tieguanyin Tea was smooth with a clean finish, and the richness of the milk provided a special cozy touch to the flavor profile. In hindsight, though, she wishes she’d opted for a cold tea with a little sugar added. Not that her hot unsweetened brew was bad, but it had turned out to be an unseasonably warm day when she visited the cafe, and something cool and sweet would have been a weather-appropriate pick-me-up.

This does mean, though, that she now has a reason to go back again and get the red teapot, since the lid toppers are yours to keep and take home with you.

title: Studio Ghibli adds new cosy socks to its anime merchandise collection

content:
The perfect partners for a cosy night in watching Ghibli movies. 

Studio Ghibli movies have a cosy, handmade feel to them, and that feeling extends to its merchandise collections, sold through the affiliated Donguri Kyowakoku retail chain.

▼ Now, the cosiness levels are being dialled up a notch for autumn, with the brand new release of two fleece-lined socks in honour of two Ghibli Movies.

Made with a fluffy, velour-like chenille yarn, the socks are soft, with excellent heat retention to warm your feet from the moment you slip into them. They also look like the perfect partners for a night in watching the movies they represent.

▼ Kiki’s Delivery Service Fleece-Lined Crew Socks, 23–25 centimetres (9.1-9.8 inches)

Beloved cat Jiji peers out from this warm pair, with its embroidered body contrasting against the pink background, and the purple in its ears pairing well with the hues.

▼ Inside is an interior so warm and fluffy that your toes will never want to leave.

▼ Whisper of the Heart Fleece-Lined Crew Socks, 23–25 centimetres (9.1-9.8 inches)

Whisper of the Heart tends to sit in the shadow of Ghibli’s more famous films, but here it takes centre stage, with feline Moon representing.

▼ Moon meets its match in terms of fluffiness with this pair.

It’s nice to see two of the studio’s famous felines bringing their charm to these anime socks, which make a nice addition to the range released last month. Both socks are priced at 1,540 yen (US$9.75) per pair and can be purchased now at Donguri Kyowakoku stores and online (links below) while stocks last.

title: Japanese food hack says to soak your grapes in carbonated water, but is the fizz worth the buzz?
description: We try a Shine Muscat experiment that method claim lets Japan’s most delicious grapes shine in a different way. Shine Muscats don’t really need to be any tastier than they already are. The extra-sweet grapes are among Japan’s most highly prized fruits, and with them in season right now, fans are, quite literally, eating well […]
content:
We try a Shine Muscat experiment that method claim lets Japan’s most delicious grapes shine in a different way.

Shine Muscats don’t really need to be any tastier than they already are. The extra-sweet grapes are among Japan’s most highly prized fruits, and with them in season right now, fans are, quite literally, eating well these days.

Of course, if someone were to figure out a way to make Shine Muscat grapes taste even better, we’d be happy to give it a try, even if it sounded kind of crazy. That’s what we recently did when we tried pickling some Shine Muscats in traditional nukadoko (fermented rice bran), and sure enough, it made their sweetness even more intensely concentrated. The results were so good, in fact, that we were planning to pickle all the rest of our Shine Muscats too, but at the last second, we set some aside for another experiment.

See, we’d also heard rumors that you can enhance your Shine Muscats with carbonated water. We’re not talking about a brief dip in a glass of soda water, either. Japanese foodies who pioneered this technique say you’ve got to let the grapes soak for a long time before you bite into them.

We were curious to try this food hack for ourselves, and the required materials/equipment make for a short list. All you need are Shine Muscat grapes, carbonated water, and a jar with a sealable lid.

Put the grapes into the jar…

…pour in enough soda water to cover them…

…then close the lid tight and let the jar sit in your refrigerator for anywhere between 12 hours and two days.

Shine Muscats are premium-priced fruit, so in the interest of not wasting any for half-effort experimentation, we were patient and held out for the full two days of soaking. When we finally took the jar back out of the fridge and opened it up, all of the carbonation had vanished from the water.

▼ Not a bubble to be seen or a fizz to be heard

We removed a grape from the jar, and set it on a place next to a control-group Shine Muscat that we hadn’t done any sort of treatment to. As you can see in the photo below, the two-day carbonated bath hadn’t done anything to change the grape’s outward appearance.

▼ Shine Muscat soaked in carbonated water for two days (left) and regulae Shine Muscat

Slicing each grape open to look at its cross section, we observed no changes to the carbonated Shine Muscat’s inner beauty either.

The rumors hadn’t said that this experiment would do anything to make the grapes look better, though. The soaking process is supposed to make the Shine Muscats more delicious, so does it? Yes and no, which might sound like faint praise, but we actually were totally satisfied.

As far as we could tell, soaking the grapes in soda water doesn’t change their flavor itself. What it does do, though, is transfer the bubbly quality into the outer layer of the Shine Muscat. Bite into one, and you’re rewarded with a burst of carbonated popping. With the Shine Muscat sweetness still fully present, it’s an incredibly refreshing combination of fun fruity fizziness.

With how simple these are to make, it’d be a snap to whip up a batch of carbonated Shine Muscats either to take to a party or to enjoy as luxurious at-home snacks for yourself. Note, though, that you’ll want to make sure to use a jar where the lid can be shut tightly, since if there’s excess slack in the seal the carbonation is going to escape into the air instead of finding a new home in your grapes.

title: One of Japan’s best convenience store egg sandwiches is one you won’t find at the big three chains

content:
Even if you can’t go every day, here’s why you should go to Daily Yamazaki today.

Japan’s big three convenience store chains, 7-Eleven, Family Mart, and Lawson, all sell fine baked goods. The bread is on an especially high level, though, at Daily Yamazaki. Of course, that’s to be expected, what with the chain being owned by Japan’s biggest baking company, Yamazaki Baking Co. So whenever we find ourselves inside a Daily Yamazaki branch, we always make sure to check out what’s stocked in the sandwich corner, and on a recent visit we found one of the best convenience store egg sandwiches we’ve ever had.

Really, most Japanese egg sandwiches could more accurately be called egg salad sandwiches, but Daily Yamazaki’s new Egg Sandwich with a Whole Boiled Egg (or Yudetamago Ikko Shiyo Tamago Sando, in Japanese) is true to its name, and immediately grabbed our attention with its mouthwatering appearance.

Three cross sections are on display, bulging out from between the slices of bread. Though it’s just a single-cut sandwich, as opposed to the more common two-slice varieties, the immense amount of fillings promised a hearty, eggy meal.

The boiled egg is sliced into three pieces, roughly a half and two quarter-sized cuts. And yes, there is egg salad here too, generous slathers that go all the way to the edges of the bread, making this a sort of hybrid-style egg sandwich.

▼ We flipped one piece of bread over to see if Daily Yamazaki skimps on the spread, and were happy to see that they do not.

Taking a bite, we were greeted with a deliciously rich, creamy mixture of egg white and egg yolk flavors, plus an invitingly engaging contrast of the melty egg salad and firmer slices of boiled egg.

It was kind of like eating two different types of egg sandwich at once, an exercise in enjoyable eggy efficiency. If you’re after a more focused experience, though, Daily Yamazaki also has an Ajiwai (“Flavorful”) Egg Sandwich, which finds room to add a dash of spicy dressing to its otherwise conventional egg salad filling, again with so much that it’s practically overflowing from the bread.

But even with the Whole Boiled Egg sandwich being a touch more expensive than the Ajiwai (334 yen [US$2.10] versus 284 yen) it’s hard to say no to something that looks and tastes so good, and we highly recommend it for your next cholesterol cheat day.
